segs.text: Module four, objective five. Calculating total, renal and hepatic clearance. Clearance, Cl, is the volume of fluid cleared of drug per unit time, so its units are a volume per time, such as liters per hour or milliliters per minute. The textbook gives an example: with a clearance of fifteen milliliters per minute and a volume of distribution, V D, of twelve liters, fifteen milliliters of the twelve liters are cleared of drug each minute.

card.m: Cl: volume cleared of drug per time, L/hr or mL/min
e.g. (textbook) Cl 15 mL/min, V<sub>D</sub> 12 L: 15 mL of the 12 L cleared each minute

segs.text: Clearance links the rate of elimination, an amount per time, to C p, the plasma concentration, an amount per volume: the rate equals clearance times C p, and the volumes cancel. In her penicillin example, fifteen milliliters per minute times five micrograms per milliliter gives seventy five micrograms per minute. As C p falls after a dose, the amount removed per minute falls with it, because the same volume is cleared each minute but it holds less drug. The clearance, the volume per minute, stays the same as long as elimination is first order. So the claim that clearance rises as concentration rises is false: a change in concentration changes the elimination rate, not the clearance.

Total clearance comes from either of two relations. Cl T equals F times D zero over A U C, where F is the bioavailability factor, one for an I V dose, and A U C is the area under the plasma concentration time curve. The dose is on the top and A U C on the bottom, so for the same dose, a larger clearance goes with a smaller A U C, because the body removes the drug faster. Cl T also equals k times V D, the elimination rate constant times the volume of distribution. k is the fraction of the drug removed per hour, so k times the volume that holds the drug is the volume cleared per hour.

card.m: same D<sub>0</sub>: Cl up → AUC down
fraction per hour × volume = volume cleared per hour
k × V<sub>D</sub>: not on the sheet, from memory

segs.text: Collecting urine until drug no longer appears gives the cumulative amount excreted unchanged, D u infinity. Divided by the dose that reached the body, F times D zero, it gives f e, the fraction excreted unchanged, which has no units. f e is also the kidney's share of the elimination rate constant: it equals k e over k, where k e is the excretion rate constant, so k e equals f e times k. The kidney's share of the clearance is the same fraction, so Cl R equals f e times Cl T, and hepatic clearance, Cl H, is the rest, one minus f e times Cl T, or Cl T minus Cl R. She said, lowercase f e is our fraction excreted, capital F is our bioavailability factor.

card.m: D<sub>u</sub><sup>∞</sup>: total unchanged drug in the urine, mg

segs.text: Her slide example: five hundred milligrams of a drug was given by rapid I V injection, the V D is fifteen liters, and the elimination half-life is eight hours. Urine was collected for forty eight hours, and three hundred milligrams of unchanged drug was recovered. Asked are f e, k, k e, Cl T, Cl R and Cl H, and f e comes first because every later term uses it. F is one for an I V dose, so f e is three hundred over five hundred milligrams, zero point six, with no units. The forty eight hours are not in the arithmetic, but they matter: forty eight hours is six half-lives, long enough that the amount collected counts as all the drug the kidney will excrete.

card.m: D<sub>0</sub> = 500 mg IV (F = 1), V<sub>D</sub> = 15 L, t½ = 8 hr
48 hr = 6 × 8 hr: the amount counts as the total excreted (textbook: at least 3 to 4 half-lives)

segs.text: Next, k comes from the half-life, because the half-life equals zero point six nine three over k. k e is f e times k, the part of k due to the kidney, and Cl T is k times V D, one point three liters per hour. Cl R is f e times Cl T, zero point seven eight liters per hour, and Cl H, by difference, is zero point five two liters per hour. So of the one point three liters of plasma cleared of drug each hour, the kidney clears six tenths and the liver four tenths.

Clearance, half-life and volume are linked. Clearance is the volume cleared per hour and V D the volume holding the drug, so their ratio, k, is the fraction removed per hour. Putting this into the half-life equals zero point six nine three over k gives the half-life equals zero point six nine three times V D over Cl T. Cl T is on the bottom, so with the volume unchanged, a lower clearance gives a longer half-life in inverse proportion, and a higher clearance gives a shorter one. V D is on the top, so at the same clearance a larger volume gives a longer half-life; in a textbook example, twice the volume gives twice the half-life. V D and Cl T must share a volume unit.

card.m: V<sub>D</sub> same: Cl<sub>T</sub> down → t½ up; Cl<sub>T</sub> up → t½ down
e.g. (textbook) Cl 125 mL/min both: V<sub>D</sub> 10 L → 55.44 min, 20 L → 110.88 min
same volume unit; not on the sheet

segs.text: Her slide example: a new antibiotic, actively secreted by the kidney, has a V D of twenty five liters and a clearance of seven hundred fifty milliliters per minute, falling to one hundred fifty in partial renal failure. The half-life line answers both questions, because V D stays the same while clearance changes. The usual half-life is twenty three point one minutes, and in renal failure it is one hundred fifteen point five minutes. Clearance fell to one fifth, so the half-life became five times longer.

Quiz three asked what happens to the elimination half-life if total body clearance increases due to renal dysfunction. The key is that the half-life decreases. Answer from the direction of clearance that the stem states, not from the cause it names: clearance up, half-life down, whatever the reason. Other traps are giving f e units, and putting the urinary fraction in place of capital F, which is one on an I V problem whatever the urine shows.

card.m: Quiz 3: Cl<sub>T</sub> increases (stem: renal dysfunction) → t½ ?
Cl<sub>T</sub> up → t½ down, whatever the cause
✗ units on f<sub>e</sub>   ✗ f<sub>e</sub> in place of F
